title: George Sivulka, Co-Founder & CEO @Hebbia: The Future of Foundation Models
author: George Sivulka

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Repeatable services: Organisational redesign changes legal delivery
st.an: Sivulka does not directly endorse the cluster’s central move from individual augmentation to repeatable legal-service delivery. He instead prioritises human augmentation, task change and narrowly defined, measurable document-analysis use cases while challenging broad enterprise-transformation claims as hype.

st.t: Legal software: Workflow layers defend specialist value
st.an: Sivulka supports the cluster’s central product-layer thesis: capable foundation models do not by themselves constitute a valuable product, and durable value can lie in a flexible, human-first layer built around them. The evidence is general rather than legal-specific and does not address lawyer–engineer collaboration, verification or professional accountability.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Sivulka supports selective, workflow-specific deployment: he distinguishes impressive demonstrations and broad usage from operational value, urges enterprises to target measurable outcomes in defined use cases, and argues that more capable agents require intelligible human interfaces. He does not directly address legal verification or professional accountability, while his broader economic forecasts remain predictive.

kp.k: Enterprise questions require analysis beyond document retrieval
kp.d: Sivulka says Hebbia's experience with financial-services customers prompted a move beyond retrieval-augmented generation: almost 90% of customer questions required work on documents rather than locating an explicitly stated answer. Examples include investment diligence, aggregating mentions of AI and identifying exposure to Silicon Valley Bank during the regional banking crisis. This is a vendor-reported observation, without a stated sample size or formal evaluation methodology.
qs: it was actually almost 90% of the questions that people were asking these systems weren't answerable by search through the doc doents but rather they had to be work done on top of the documents
it's not actually finding something that exists already it's taking all the things that exist already and starting to answer questions about that information

kp.k: Contract analysis illustrates ambiguous, higher-skilled agentic work
kp.d: Sivulka contrasts simple robotic process automation with requests involving 800-page credit agreements or 230-page confidential information memorandums. Users ask for inconsistencies and events of default rather than merely copied numbers. He describes Hebbia as addressing high-level, ambiguous decision-making while tracing decisions to citations or individual characters; he does not provide measured accuracy or describe a human verification protocol.
qs: some of the things that people are asking heia are over 800 page credit agreements or 230 page you know Sims uh confidential information memorandums
tell me uh what are inconsistencies in this document tell me where there's an event of default that we can trigger
ambiguous decision-making and trying to trace it all the way down back to individual citations or individual characters that led the model to that decision

kp.k: Orchestration scales inference across many smaller model calls
kp.d: Sivulka claims Hebbia pioneered an orchestration approach roughly a year to 18 months earlier: decomposing a question into hundreds or thousands of model operations across documents rather than waiting for larger foundation models. He distinguishes this from OpenAI o1's repeated reasoning within a model and asserts improved accuracy and capacity for complex problems, without supplying comparative test results.
qs: heia Matrix orchestrates lots of smaller llm calls
for simple single question let's actually run hundreds or even thousands of submodels of the best models in the world to to compute over every single document to answer the same question
you could take whatever state-of-the-art or Cutting Edge and run it more times to get more compute

kp.k: Model selection varies by document and task
kp.d: Sivulka describes Hebbia as model-agnostic, combining major providers and some proprietary models. He reports that Anthropic works better on some dense legal or colloquial documents, whereas OpenAI models perform better on others. Task decomposition can combine OpenAI, Anthropic and Gemini, with trade-offs between accuracy and speed. These are vendor observations rather than independent legal-model evaluations.
qs: we are completely model agnostic
we've seen that for certain types of documents like the dense legal Le or or or even um more colloquial documents anthropic works better
it's always trade-offs between accuracy and speed and all kinds of things actually a lot of the time when we're decomposing a task we'll use mixes of open AI anthropic even Gemini

kp.k: General scaling may outperform domain-specialised model training
kp.d: Sivulka uses Bloomberg GPT as an example of a specialised model allegedly overtaken by GPT-4 despite Bloomberg's financial data advantage; he explicitly expresses uncertainty about release timing. He predicts inference scaling will similarly outpace fine-tuning. His view that high-quality training data is approaching constraints is expressly a gut feeling, not a data-collection finding.
qs: it just destroyed Bloomberg GPT at every single Finance task
nothing that that other players can do to find tune models will ever catch up
that's a that's a gut feel I'm not you know I'm not looking at uh I'm not particularly in data collection myself

kp.d: Sivulka estimates that 90% of the market remains in the experimental-budget phase and criticises demonstrations that fail on real-world questions. He recommends concentrating on specific, repeatable use cases with measurable value. The percentage and critique are his market assessments, not results from a documented survey.
qs: I think that 90% of the market is still in experimental budget phase but we're starting to see early Promises of actual value
my entire business is focused on on just those repeatable use cases
change will take time

kp.k: Revenue opportunities can accelerate otherwise slow enterprise adoption
kp.d: Responding to the host's report of Daniel Dines's warning about slow enterprise adoption, Sivulka distinguishes cost-cutting from generating outsized investment value. He argues finance can adopt rapidly when a tool delivers alpha, citing Excel's claimed 90% penetration in 1985–1986 over 18 to 24 months and a later two-year adoption period for credit-card data in public-company valuation. These are historical analogies asserted in the interview.
qs: Excel went to 90% Market penetration in finance 1985 to 1986 literally 18 months to 24 months
unless you're providing outsized alpha or real value in which case the minute that there's something real Finance moves faster than any other industry

kp.k: AI may expand juniors' access to institutional experience
kp.d: The host worries that automating junior analytical work removes the apprenticeship pathway for future senior decision-makers. Sivulka disagrees, arguing that juniors can compare a company against every historical deal rather than rely on a senior investor's recollection of 20 comparable transactions. His hypothetical example presents AI as augmentation of investment judgment, not evidence that training losses have been measured or resolved.
qs: we have this no graduation pathway for the next generation
you might have remembered 20 deals but I'm looking through every deal in our company's history in a giant Matrix
it allows them to be better investors

kp.k: Routine execution shifts toward managing AI juniors
kp.d: Sivulka predicts that lower-cognition back-office, middle-office and some junior front-office tasks will move from manual execution to managing AI juniors. He expects firms using the technology to increase assets under management and employment rather than simply shrink teams, drawing an analogy to Excel. These are optimistic labour-market predictions; the interview supplies no employment study.
qs: I genuinely believe that uh it'll actually increase the AUM of the firms that use it I think it will actually drive more employment
the cognitive tasks that are lower in cognition I.E like more back office kind of middle office uh maybe even some of the more Junior front office tasks
how can we manage AI Juniors rather than uh you know actually do this ourselves by hand

kp.k: More capable agents increase human-facing management needs
kp.d: Sivulka rejects the host's reported proposition that business applications will all collapse into agents. He expects platforms, applications and agent employees to coexist. He also argues that chat is only a limited interface and that deploying thousands of expert agents creates an orchestration and management problem requiring understandable, human-centred interfaces.
qs: I ultimately think that it will be a mix of of all three
the better agents are the more work that they do the more important it will be that they are easily understood by you humans
actually it becomes a management problem right there's this whole infrastructure orchestration layer

kp.k: Business expertise and behavioural change constrain implementation
kp.d: Sivulka argues that people closest to business work, rather than CTOs or IT personnel, are best positioned to identify useful AI applications. He proposes platforms that let business users discover workflows and identifies adoption and change management as harder than the technology itself. This is his implementation argument, not a comparison based on measured deployment outcomes.
qs: the people that that actually understand how to use AI in a business context are those that are closest to the business
the hardest part of AI change management no matter what company you are are people and like actually getting people to use the software

kp.k: Per-seat pricing aims to encourage intensive AI use
kp.d: Sivulka discusses consumption, per-seat, employee-salary-like and flat pricing as possible agent business models. He explains Hebbia's per-seat approach as both human-centred and aligned with business users' purchasing habits. He argues that charging per interaction penalises experimentation and behavioural change, whereas a fixed seat fee encourages greater use. This concerns software-vendor pricing, not legal fees.
qs: business users like to pay per seat because it's how they how they map back to Value
when you charge for consumption or API pricing you're disincentivizing the change
versus here's a per seat fee it might be expensive but use it more

kp.k: Falling inference costs support compute-intensive application economics
kp.d: Sivulka claims inference cost over a fixed parameter count fell by roughly seven orders of magnitude in four years since Hebbia started. He argues this makes extensive orchestration economically attractive and says margins improve quarterly. The claim is vendor-reported and accompanied by no cost series or margin figures.
qs: the cost of of of inference over fixed number number of parameters has decreased in by like seven orders of magnitude in four years
every single quarter like our margin goes we're not spending money fast enough

kp.k: Commoditised models may shift value toward applications and infrastructure
kp.d: Sivulka predicts foundation-model commoditisation, with greater value accruing to infrastructure and application or agent layers. He contrasts relatively easy model switching with cloud migration, which he estimates could cost a substantially sized startup $10 million to $20 million. He treats switching costs as a reason model provision may not reproduce cloud providers' durable economics.
qs: the model layer and I think this is not a hot take anymore I've been saying it for a few years but I think it will become commoditized
it will be the infrastructure layer and then actually the application or agent layer that will acre the most value ultimately
a 10 million to $20 million investment just to switch

kp.k: Inference growth could weaken Nvidia's training-based advantage
kp.d: Sivulka attributes Nvidia's advantage partly to researchers' familiarity with CUDA rather than technology alone. He predicts that moving more computation toward inference will create opportunities for AMD, large technology providers and custom chips because deployed models can run on cheaper infrastructure. He remains bullish on Nvidia while expressing greater relative enthusiasm for alternative inference suppliers.
qs: people H and networks have the most friction to change
you have your academics and your researchers you know training large models on Nvidia chips but the minute they deploy them they can deploy them uh on cheaper infrastructure
I'm actually still bullish on Nvidia but I'm even more bullish on other chip makers

kp.k: Human habits can protect incumbent software businesses
kp.d: Sivulka argues that AI's ability to build software does not eliminate incumbent advantages. Discussing Salesforce, he identifies habitual use and the difficulty of changing human behaviour as substantial switching barriers. He disputes promotional claims that AI-generated replacements necessarily make established enterprise applications obsolete.
qs: the switching cost the network effect of changing human beings habits is too high
Salesforce is one of those kind of like monopolies in that they have so much stickiness habitual stickiness

kp.k: Long-run growth forecasts underpin an expansive market thesis
kp.d: Sivulka predicts $100 trillion in additional value over the next 60 years from AI or inference and believes agentic applications will contribute more than 50% of GDP in the next few decades. He uses computing's historical economic impact as an analogy and expects gains for both AI suppliers and legacy businesses that adopt effectively. He acknowledges his techno-optimism; these are speculative forecasts, not modelled estimates.
qs: I actually think a hundred trillion dollar of value will be created uh in the next 60 years
I believe it will be additional value and maybe I'm too techno Optimist
more than 50% of the GDP will be contributed by what you can call agentic applications in the next few decades

kp.k: Government demand and energy access shape model competition
kp.d: Sivulka predicts governments will be major AI users and argues that energy availability and geopolitical positioning matter to model development and deployment. He speculates that xAI could overtake OpenAI and Anthropic in value within 12 to 24 months, citing Elon Musk's operational efficiency and positioning. He separately calls for clear industry guardrails without proposing specific legal or professional rules.
qs: governments will be some of the largest users of AI
energy is a very big bottleneck
xai might overtake open Ai and enth thropic in value uh over the next you know 12 to 24 months
we as an industry have very clear guard rails uh that we can follow and and understand

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Sivulka predicts that AI agents will augment financial-services professionals, enable more complex document analysis, and create substantial economic value; he also predicts shifts in AI platforms, models and infrastructure.
pts.d: This is primarily a cross-domain source about financial services and enterprise AI, not a forecast about law-firm staffing or legal markets. George Sivulka claims that retrieval-based systems are inadequate for many investment questions because users need analysis across documents rather than retrieval of explicit statements. He positions Hebbia as performing higher-level, ambiguous analysis, including identifying inconsistencies and potential events of default in credit agreements, with decisions traced to citations. He argues that access to a firm's entire deal history can make junior investors better informed, rather than deprive them of development opportunities. He predicts increased assets under management and employment at adopting firms, while lower-cognition back-office, middle-office and some junior front-office work shifts toward managing AI juniors. He expects platforms, applications and agents to coexist, and argues that more capable agents make human-facing management interfaces more important. He predicts $100 trillion in additional value over 60 years and more than half of GDP coming from agentic applications within the next few decades. Technically, he claims that orchestrating many model calls improves accuracy and complexity-handling, predicts model-layer commoditisation and greater value capture by infrastructure and applications, and anticipates a shift toward inference benefiting alternative chipmakers. He argues that human habits and switching costs can protect incumbent enterprise software. He presents per-seat pricing as encouraging adoption rather than penalising usage.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists mainly of Sivulka's account of Hebbia deployments, internal usage observations and technical experience, supplemented by historical analogies; the transcript supplies no independently documented tests of these claims.
pts.d: For retrieval limitations, Sivulka cites deployment at large financial firms and an examination of customer queries, reporting that almost 90% required work on top of documents rather than search alone. He reports reaching $1 million in revenue sometime in 2021 or 2022. For orchestration, he describes running hundreds or thousands of submodels over documents and claims superior accuracy, without giving a benchmark, sample, error rate or comparison protocol. He reports that Anthropic performs better on some dense legal and colloquial documents, while OpenAI performs better on others, and says Hebbia mixes providers according to accuracy and speed. He claims inference costs for a fixed parameter count fell by roughly seven orders of magnitude in four years, without providing a calculation or data source. His workforce and adoption predictions rely on analogies to Excel and financial firms' uptake of alternative data, plus a hypothetical junior investor using historical deal information. His macroeconomic forecasts are extrapolations from computing's economic impact, not a presented economic model. He explicitly describes his view about approaching limits to high-quality training data as a gut feeling. His assertions that approximately 90% of enterprise AI remains experimental and that much usage is overstated are not accompanied by a survey methodology.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Sivulka distinguishes current experimental adoption and limited repeatable use cases from longer-term transformation, with speed dependent on useful products, business value and human adoption.
pts.d: He dates Hebbia's early retrieval work to 2020 and its initial revenue growth to sometime in 2021 or 2022. He describes inference orchestration as developed roughly a year to 18 months before the interview. His current-value claims are restricted to specific, defined, repeatable use cases; he says 90% of the market is still using experimental budgets. Rapid adoption is conditional on delivering outsized investment returns or real value and on packaging the technology in a useful product. He identifies people and change management, rather than technology alone, as the hardest adoption constraint. When challenged with a five-year replacement horizon, he maintains an augmentation and employment-growth position, but does not give a dated workforce estimate. His economic horizons are the next few decades for agentic applications exceeding half of GDP and the next 60 years for $100 trillion of additional value, later comparing AI's effects with a 60–80-year computing transition. He separately predicts that xAI might overtake OpenAI and Anthropic in value within 12–24 months, conditional on operational efficiency and geopolitical positioning. Model and chip-market shifts have no precise completion date. Relative dates should be read as relative to the interview; the supplied document is labelled 2026.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The directly affected groups are investment firms, junior and senior investment professionals, enterprise business users and AI suppliers; legal relevance is confined mainly to document-analysis tasks.
pts.d: Investment banks, private-equity firms and other financial institutions are presented as buyers gaining analytical capacity, better investment decisions and potentially higher assets under management. Junior investors gain access to institutional deal histories that can supplement or challenge senior investors' remembered experience. Back-office, middle-office and some junior front-office staff are expected to move from manual cognitive work toward supervising AI. Business users are positioned as better placed than IT teams to identify valuable applications, while managers need interfaces for coordinating agent work. Users analysing long credit agreements may identify inconsistencies or default provisions, but the transcript does not establish effects on lawyers, client fees, law-firm leverage or access to justice. Hebbia is presented as a software platform, not an alternative legal service provider delivering legal work. Foundation-model suppliers face easier switching and commoditisation; application and infrastructure providers may capture greater value. Nvidia retains advantages in training, while AMD, large technology companies and custom-chip providers may benefit from inference demand. Existing enterprise software providers such as Salesforce may remain protected by habitual switching costs. Sivulka also anticipates benefits for non-AI businesses that use the technology effectively.
